text: Table 2 shows that, on ordered electricity data, improving coverage through calibration weighting need not require wider intervals once fitting also changes. At a 90% target, ordinary full conformal with least squares (CP+LS) averages 85.2% coverage and width 0.565. Weighting only calibration residuals (NexCP+LS) raises coverage to 89.0% but increases width to 0.606. Adding weighted least-squares fitting (NexCP+WLS) retains higher coverage, 89.3%, while reducing width to 0.527, below both alternatives; neither weighted method reaches 90% on average. Uniform random permutation makes the data exchangeable: the respective coverages are 89.9%, 90.8%, and 90.8%, with widths 0.639, 0.652, and 0.663. The fitting change thus offers no width advantage in this control, and weighted procedures have greater variability. This contrast supports distinct calibration and fitting benefits in the ordered setting, not a generally narrower weighted method. These averages across prediction times neither establish coverage at every time nor universal 90% coverage under drift, because the theorem's weighted swapped-residual total-variation penalty may be large.

Table 2 distinguishes improved calibration from narrower intervals on the ordered electricity-transfer data. Keeping least-squares fitting fixed, weighting calibration residuals raises coverage from 85.2% to 89.0% but increases mean width from 0.565 to 0.606. Retaining residual weighting and adding weighted least-squares fitting gives 89.3% coverage and reduces width to 0.527, below the unweighted baseline's 0.565. Thus calibration weighting improves coverage here at a width cost, while weighted fitting offsets that cost; neither weighted method reaches the 90% target. Uniformly permuting the same data creates an exchangeable control: coverage is 89.9%, 90.8%, and 90.8% for unweighted, residual-weighted, and additionally weighted-fit methods, respectively, with widths 0.639, 0.652, and 0.663. The observed width advantage disappears after permutation. These time-averaged comparisons do not guarantee 90% coverage under arbitrary drift: the theoretical lower bound is near nominal only when the weighted total-variation discrepancy between original and swapped residual-vector distributions is small.

Theorem 2b fixes calibration weights w_i in [0,1] and algorithm tags before observing data. Normalize the weights with a unit test weight and draw K independently using these probabilities. At the true label, fitting after swapping observations K and n+1 while keeping tags fixed puts the test residual at index K of R(Z^K). For any residual vector r, indices S(r) strictly above its weighted (1-alpha)-quantile have normalized weight at most alpha. Because the test weight dominates every calibration weight, the prediction cutoff with test mass at infinity is no smaller than the cutoff for R(Z^K); miscoverage therefore implies K belongs to S(R(Z^K)). Independence expresses this event probability as a weighted sum over K. Replacing each swapped residual law by the original costs at most its total-variation distance. The original-law sum is at most alpha, yielding miscoverage at most alpha plus the weighted residual-distribution penalty.

Full conformal prediction usually relies on exchangeable data and symmetric fitting, excluding order-sensitive predictors and leaving coverage vulnerable to drift. Our extension separates two roles: fixed calibration weights in [0,1] emphasize observations expected to resemble the test point, while fixed algorithm tags encode information used by nonsymmetric fitting. A data-independent weighted random swap moves the candidate test point to a sampled position before fitting, with tags retained at their positions. This makes miscoverage imply membership in a high-residual set with weighted mass at most alpha. Comparing swapped and original residual-vector distributions yields finite-sample coverage at least 1 - alpha minus their weighted total-variation discrepancy. Under exchangeability this discrepancy vanishes even with nonsymmetric fitting; otherwise, a small discrepancy bounds undercoverage, not exact nominal validity. With distinct residuals, small discrepancy and normalized test weight also limit overcoverage; related bounds extend to split conformal and jackknife+. Simulations and electricity data distinguish calibration gains from width gains: on ordered electricity data, residual weighting improves coverage but widens intervals, whereas adding weighted fitting gives 89.3% coverage and narrower intervals than unweighted fitting, against a 90% target. Permutation removes the width advantage, and election-data coverage also remains below target.

We extend full conformal prediction to nonexchangeable data and nonsymmetric model fitting, with related split conformal and jackknife+ procedures. Prespecified calibration weights in [0,1] reduce reliance on observations considered less comparable to the test point, while fixed algorithm tags allow fitting to use order or regression weights. A data-independent swap, sampled with probabilities proportional to these weights and a unit test weight, makes miscoverage imply membership in a high-residual set of normalized weight at most alpha. Comparing swapped and original residual distributions then gives finite-sample coverage at least 1-alpha minus their weighted total-variation distances, without requiring fitting symmetry. Exchangeability eliminates this penalty; under nonexchangeability, a small penalty bounds undercoverage, with distinct residuals and small normalized test weight additionally limiting overcoverage. Experiments distinguish calibration from fitting: on ordered electricity data, residual weighting improves coverage but widens intervals, whereas weighted least squares narrows intervals while retaining the coverage improvement. Random permutation removes this width advantage, and election coverage improves but remains below the 90% target. Thus the guarantee depends on residual-distribution changes, while empirical benefits depend on the evaluated ordering and weighting choices.

Weighted quantiles and nonsymmetric fitting prevent the usual exchangeable-rank argument. Prespecify calibration weights w_i in [0,1] and algorithm tags; normalize by D = 1 + sum_i w_i, assigning test weight 1/D. Draw K independently of the data using these normalized weights, swap the candidate test point with position K, and fit with tags fixed at their positions. At the true response, the test residual becomes entry K of the swapped-sequence residual vector. Replacing the test residual by infinity and using the test weight's dominance over calibration weights show that miscoverage implies entry K exceeds that vector's weighted (1 - alpha)-quantile. Such high-residual indices have total normalized weight at most alpha for every vector. Independence allows averaging their probabilities over K. Total variation bounds the change in each probability between swapped and original residual-vector distributions, yielding miscoverage at most alpha plus the weighted discrepancy, without fitting symmetry or stability.
